Deadass
DED-as
adverb / adjective (Gen-Z slang, NYC origin)
New York slang (decades old locally; nationalized by social media in the late 2010s-2020s): "completely serious" — an emphasis-oath certifying that the speaker is not joking: "I'm deadass," "deadass the best slice in Brooklyn."

Biblical Definition

Deadass is a sincerity-certificate: dropped before or after a claim, it swears the speaker is completely serious. ("Deadass?" / "Deadass." is an entire verified exchange.) Parents should hear two things in it. First, the obvious: it carries a coarse fragment, and a tongue trained toward grace finds cleaner tools (Eph 4:29; Col 4:6). Second, the subtler and more interesting thing: the word exists because ordinary speech has stopped being believed. A generation marinated in irony, exaggeration, and engagement-bait must now NOTARIZE its sentences — deadass, no cap, fr fr, on God — a whole stack of mini-oaths to purchase what a plain word once carried. The Lord's teaching lands on this stack with precision: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil (Matt 5:37). The escalation of oaths is the inflation of a devalued currency — and the devaluation is the real story. The Christian alternative is not a holier intensifier but a reputation: a man whose plain yes has never needed a notary. Let him say a thing once, unadorned, and be believed — that is the quiet glory the whole deadass economy is bankrupt for.

DEADASS, adv./adj. (NYC slang, nationalized late 2010s–present) Completely serious; not joking: "I'm deadass."

"Deadass?" / "Deadass." functions as a complete claim-and-verification exchange.

Belongs to the sincerity-oath stack: no cap, on God, fr fr, I swear.

Carries a coarse fragment; cleaner tools exist for a tongue trained toward grace.

Decode for parents: the word exists because plain speech stopped being believed — that is the story.

Key Scripture

Matt 5:37 — "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil."

Jas 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

Eph 4:29 — "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers."

Col 4:6 — "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man."

Modern Corruption

A sincerity-oath for a low-trust speech economy: when every sentence performs, plain words need notarizing. The oath-stack is inflation; the cure is a yes that has never lied.

expand to see more

The trust deficit. Deadass, no cap, on God, fr fr — the young carry more oath-instruments than a medieval court, and for the same reason courts needed them: the default assumption is exaggeration. Christ's teaching in Matt 5 was aimed at exactly such a stack (by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by thy head) — graded oaths that let speech be mostly worthless and occasionally guaranteed. His remedy was not a better oath but the abolition of the tiers: ALL your words should be the reliable kind.

The coarse fragment and the cleaner tongue. The word's tail is crude, and Christians need not pretend otherwise: out of the same mouth ought not proceed blessing and coarseness (Eph 4:29; Jas 3:10). But the deeper discipleship issue is the economy it serves. Raise young people whose plain sentences are collateralized by their character — whose yes has simply never bounced — and the entire notarizing apparatus becomes unnecessary in their mouths. That is not prudishness; it is wealth.
